title: Maximum Product Subarray
directAnswer: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest product. Unlike Kadane's max-sum, you must track BOTH the running max AND the running min ending here — because a negative number flips the smallest (most-negative) product into the largest. One pass, swap max/min when the current number is negative, O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Kadane with a twist — carry max AND min
remember.formula:
curMax = curMin = best = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
    if x < 0: curMax, curMin = curMin, curMax
    curMax = max(x, curMax * x)
    curMin = min(x, curMin * x)
    best = max(best, curMax)
rules: Track **both** `curMax` and `curMin` ending at i — a negative number turns the most-negative product into the most-positive.
When `nums[i] < 0`, **swap** `curMax` and `curMin` *before* multiplying — the roles reverse.
Always include `nums[i]` itself as a fresh start: `curMax = max(nums[i], curMax * nums[i])` — this resets after a zero.
A **zero** wipes both running products to 0; starting fresh at `nums[i]` handles it for free, no special case.
Seed all three (`best`, `curMax`, `curMin`) from `nums[0]`, then iterate from index 1 — never seed from 0 or 1.
whenToUse: Maximize a contiguous subarray under a non-additive op (product) where sign matters
The combine step can flip best↔worst depending on the current element
You need O(n) one-pass and the array has negatives and/or zeros
Kadane-shaped problem but the monotonicity of 'bigger is always better' breaks
antiSignals: Maximize a SUM, not a product → plain Kadane, track only the max
All elements positive → it's just the whole-array product, no min needed
Need the indices/the subarray itself, not just the value → extend with bookkeeping
remember.takeaway: The insight is that with products, the worst (most negative) running value is a future champion waiting for the next negative number to flip it. Carry both extremes and a sign flip costs nothing. This 'track min too' idea recurs anywhere a transform can invert ordering.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize plain Kadane fails on products because negatives invert ordering — and whether you fix it by carrying the running minimum alongside the maximum.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Tracking only the max (Kadane for sums) and getting [-2, 3, -4] wrong, or mishandling zeros by not allowing a fresh restart at nums[i].
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the negative-flips-sign insight explicitly, handle zeros via the max(nums[i], …) reset rather than a special case, and collapse to O(1) space with two scalars.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, find a **contiguous non-empty subarray** within the array that has the **largest product**, and return *the product*.

The test cases are generated so that the answer fits in a **32-bit integer**.

A **subarray** is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements within an array.
constraints: The product of any prefix is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer
The subarray must be contiguous and non-empty
understanding: Slide a window of contiguous elements and maximize their product. The catch versus max-sum is the sign: two negatives multiply to a positive, and a single zero resets everything. So 'the best ending here' can come from the *worst* ending one step back.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain negative numbers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole point. Two negatives make a positive, so the running minimum can become the maximum after a negative.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can it contain zeros?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A zero resets the product; the cleanest handling is to allow starting a new subarray at nums[i], which naturally recovers after a zero.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the subarray contiguous?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, contiguous and non-empty. If subsequences were allowed it would be a different problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the product overflow?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem guarantees the answer fits in 32 bits, so in Java I don't need long. In Python integers are arbitrary precision anyway.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2, 3] has product 6. The -2 then 4 can't beat it because of the lone negative.
Any subarray spanning the 0 is 0; the best non-zero options (-2, -1) are negative, so 0 wins.
The whole array: -2 × 3 × -4 = 24. The two negatives multiply to a positive — only tracking the min captures this.

diagrams.title: Why plain Kadane breaks
diagrams.caption: Sum-Kadane is monotone (bigger prefix is always at least as good); product-Kadane is not, because a negative inverts the ordering.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Every Subarray Product
approaches.whenToMention: State it to set the O(n²) baseline and to make the redundant re-multiplication obvious before optimizing.
hints: The literal task is 'largest product over all contiguous subarrays'. How many subarrays are there, and how do you get each product cheaply?
Fix a start i, then extend an end j rightward, multiplying nums[j] into a running product as you go. Track the global max.
Two nested loops: outer over start i, inner over end j ≥ i carrying the product. ~n²/2 subarrays, O(1) per extension.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n start positions × up to n extensions each, O(1) multiply per step → O(n²) time. Only a running product and a global max → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
For every start index `i`, extend the end `j` to the right, keeping a running product, and update the global maximum at each step.

**Why it's the right baseline to state.** The problem is 'best over all contiguous subarrays', and the no-insight version enumerates all of them. By carrying a running product as `j` advances (rather than recomputing the whole product each time), each subarray costs O(1) to evaluate, so the total is O(n²) — quadratic, not cubic. Saying this out loud shows you can optimize *within* brute force before reaching for the linear trick.

**What it reveals.** Watch what happens at a sign change: extending across a negative number can turn a large positive running product into a large negative one — and extending again across another negative flips it back to large positive. Brute force 'sees' this only because it tries every start independently. The O(n) solution has to *remember* that flip with a single carried value, which motivates tracking the running minimum.

**Why we don't ship it.** For n = 2 × 10⁴, O(n²) is 4 × 10⁸ operations — sluggish and a signal you didn't spot the linear structure. Mention it, give the bound, then move to the one-pass max/min scan.
approaches.insight: Re-multiplying from scratch for each (i, j) would be O(n³); carrying the product as you extend the end makes it O(n²). That 'carry the partial result' move is itself a mini-DP, and it's the gateway to realizing you can carry just one or two values across the *whole* array.

diagrams.title: Running product from start i=0
diagrams.caption: Extending across -2 flips the running product negative — the sign-flip the O(n) method must remember.

edgeCases.behavior: Single subarray, product = -3; best = -3. Confirms non-empty and seeding from MIN_VALUE.

pitfalls: Initializing best to 0 — wrong when every subarray is negative (e.g. [-3]).
Recomputing the full product for each (i, j) — turns O(n²) into O(n³).
Forgetting that the inner product can legitimately be negative; don't clamp it.

approaches.name: One Pass — Track Max AND Min (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the insight: 'a negative number turns the smallest product into the largest, so I carry both.'
hints: Kadane works for sums because a bigger running sum is always at least as useful. Why does that reasoning fail for products?
Because multiplying by a negative flips ordering: the most-negative product becomes the most-positive. So the running MINIMUM matters — keep it too.
Carry curMax and curMin ending at i. When nums[i] is negative, swap them before multiplying. Always allow nums[i] alone as a fresh start (handles zeros).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass, O(1) work per element (two multiplies, a couple of comparisons) → O(n) time. Three scalars (best, curMax, curMin) → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Carry two values as you scan: `curMax` and `curMin`, the largest and smallest products of a subarray *ending at the current index*. Update the global `best` from `curMax` each step.

**Why one running value isn't enough.** Kadane's max-sum keeps only the running maximum because addition is order-preserving: if `a ≥ b` then `a + x ≥ b + x`, so the best prefix stays the best. Multiplication breaks this. Multiply by a negative `x` and the inequality *reverses*: the smallest (most negative) product suddenly becomes the largest. So the candidate for 'best ending here' might come from the *worst* product ending one step back. The fix is to remember both extremes.

**The update, and why the swap.** At each element the new `curMax` is the best of three options: start fresh at `nums[i]`, extend the previous max (`curMax * nums[i]`), or extend the previous min (`curMin * nums[i]`). When `nums[i] < 0`, multiplying flips which of the previous two is bigger — so we **swap** `curMax` and `curMin` before applying `curMax = max(nums[i], curMax * nums[i])` and `curMin = min(nums[i], curMin * nums[i])`. The swap is just a clean way to keep the formulas the same regardless of sign.

**Why the fresh-start term handles zeros for free.** Including `nums[i]` itself in the max/min (not only the extended products) means that after a zero — which forces both `curMax` and `curMin` to 0 — the next element restarts the subarray at itself rather than being stuck multiplying by 0. No special-casing of zero is needed; the `max(nums[i], …)` term *is* the restart.

**Seeding.** Initialize all three from `nums[0]` and iterate from index 1. Seeding `best` from 0 or 1 is a classic bug — it makes all-negative or single-negative inputs wrong (the answer can legitimately be negative).
approaches.insight: The whole trick is recognizing that with products the *minimum* is a latent maximum: one negative number away from becoming the best. Carry the worst case so a future sign flip can promote it. Any time a transformation can invert ordering, tracking both extremes is the move — this is the conceptual cousin of Kadane, not a separate species.

dryRun.intro: curMax/curMin = products ending here. Swap on negatives. best follows curMax. Seed all from nums[0] = -2.

java.line: int curMax = nums[0], curMin = nums[0], best = nums[0];
java.explanation: Seed all three from the first element — never from 0 or 1, or negatives break.
A negative multiplier flips ordering, so the roles of max and min reverse.
Best ending here is either a fresh start at x or extending the previous best — the 'x' term is the zero-reset.
Global answer only ever needs the running max.

python.explanation: Swap before multiplying so the same max/min formulas work for both signs.
Python tuple swap — the most-negative product is about to become the most-positive.
max(x, …) lets the subarray restart at x, which is exactly how a zero recovers.

diagrams.title: Min becomes max after the second negative
diagrams.caption: In [-2, 3, -4], the running min (-6) at index 1 is promoted to the answer 24 when multiplied by -4.

edgeCases.behavior: At the 0 both curMax and curMin become 0 (max(0, …)). The -1 restarts at itself. best stays 0 — the correct answer.
Seed best = curMax = curMin = -2; loop never runs; returns -2. Why seeding from nums[0] (not 0) matters.

pitfalls: Tracking only curMax — fails on [-2, 3, -4] (returns 3 instead of 24).
Multiplying before swapping on a negative — applies the formulas to the wrong extremes.
Seeding best/curMax/curMin to 0 or 1 instead of nums[0] — breaks all-negative and single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Using plain Kadane (max only) and missing that two negatives make a positive.
Forgetting to swap curMax and curMin when the current element is negative.
Seeding the accumulators to 0 or 1 instead of nums[0], breaking negative-only arrays.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Tracking only the maximum
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Products invert under negatives, so the running minimum can become the maximum. Keeping only curMax returns 3 on [-2, 3, -4] instead of 24.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cur_max = best = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
    cur_max = max(x, cur_max * x)   # min never tracked
    best = max(best, cur_max)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
cur_max = cur_min = best = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
    if x < 0:
        cur_max, cur_min = cur_min, cur_max
    cur_max = max(x, cur_max * x)
    cur_min = min(x, cur_min * x)
    best = max(best, cur_max)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Multiplying before swapping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a negative element the max and min roles reverse. If you multiply first and swap after, curMax and curMin are computed from the wrong predecessors.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong seed value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Seeding best to 0 makes all-negative arrays return 0; seeding to 1 invents a product no subarray has. The first real element is the only correct seed.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int best = nums[0], curMax = nums[0], curMin = nums[0];

patternNote: Kadane-with-two-states. When maximizing a contiguous subarray under an operation that can invert ordering (multiplication, sign flips), carry both the running best and running worst. Sibling of Maximum Subarray; the min-tracking idea generalizes to any order-inverting transform.
